facts.statement: Dapedium had skin covered with thick ganoid scales.
facts.quote: The skin was covered with thick ganoid scales.

facts.statement: Dapedium possessed a robust mandible with marginal teeth that were slender, single-cusped, or two-cusped.
facts.quote: The mandible was robustly built and the marginal teeth at the edge of the mouth composed of styliform (relatively elongate and slender) teeth either being single cusped or bicusped (bearing two cusps).

facts.statement: Dapedium had smaller teeth on interior jaw and skull bones, including those on the vomer less than 1 mm across, forming dense batteries.
facts.quote: In the interior of the mouth, including on the prearticular and coronoid bones of the lower jaw and the vomer, palatoquadrate, dermopalatine and possibly the entopterygoid bones of the skull bore smaller teeth, with those on the vomer being less than 1 mm across, with the dense covering of small teeth forming batteries.

facts.statement: Dapedium lived from the Late Triassic to the Middle Jurassic (late Norian to early Aalenian) and was one of the most abundant fossil fish in Early Jurassic European deposits.
facts.quote: Dapedium lived in the Late Triassic to the Middle Jurassic period, from the late Norian to the early Aalenian, being one of the most abundant fossil fish found in Early Jurassic deposits in Europe.

facts.statement: Dapedium lived in the western Tethys Ocean surrounding Europe, with fossils found in Italy, the UK, France, Germany, and Hungary.
facts.quote: Dapedium lived in the waters of the western Tethys Ocean surrounding Europe. Remains of Dapedium species have been found in Italy, the United Kingdom (including Lyme Regis, Dorset), France, Germany and Hungary.

facts.statement: The genus Dapedium was named by William Elford Leach in 1822, with the type species D. politum described from Early Jurassic remains in Lyme Regis, Dorset, England.
facts.quote: The genus Dapedium was named by William Elford Leach in 1822, with the type species being D. politum named from remains from the Early Jurassic Lower Lias of Lyme Regis in Dorset, England.

facts.statement: Dapedium was relatively rare during the Triassic but experienced a large burst in diversification following the Triassic-Jurassic extinction event.
facts.quote: Dapedium appears to have been relatively rare during the Triassic, especially compared to other members of its family, but saw a large burst in diversification in the wake of the Triassic-Jurassic extinction event.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Dapedium survived the Triassic-Jurassic extinction event because it was a heavily-scaled generalist, unlike most Triassic dapediids which had specialized feeding or less armor.
facts.quote: It is thought that most Triassic dapediids had highly specialized feeding strategies or had less armor compared to the heavily-scaled, generalist Dapedium, allowing it to survive the extinction event.

facts.statement: Adaptations in Dapedium may have helped it survive the Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event, though its abundance declined dramatically around that time and it went extinct shortly after.
facts.quote: These adaptations may have also enabled Dapedium to survive a second extinction event, the Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event, although the abundance of Dapedium saw a dramatic decline around the time of the TOAE, and it went extinct shortly afterwards.

facts.statement: Dapedium is thought to have been a durophagous predator that used slender marginal teeth to grasp prey and smaller interior teeth to crush hard-shelled organisms.
facts.quote: Dapedium is thought to have been durophagous predator that was capable of consuming hard shelled organisms, using its slender marginal teeth to grasp and manipulate prey, before crushing them between the smaller teeth in the interior of the mouth.

facts.statement: Dapedium likely engaged in scavenging, evidenced by a specimen found inside the body cavity of the ammonite Lytoceras, where it likely became stuck while trying to scavenge.
facts.quote: Species of Dapedium likely engaged in scavenging, as indicated by the finding of a specimen of Dapedium of indeterminate species within the body cavity of the ammonite Lytoceras, which the Dapedium had likely become stuck in and died in an attempt to scavenge.

facts.statement: The monophyly of the genus Dapedium is debated, with some studies suggesting it is probably paraphyletic.
facts.quote: The monophyly of the genus has been questioned, with a number of studies suggesting the genus is probably paraphyletic.
